spatial_claims.claim: D is the midpoint of chord AC, lying on segment AC
B is on the arc of segment ABC where the perpendicular from D meets the arc (above chord AC, not on line AC)
DB is perpendicular to AC at D
E is the midpoint of segment AB, lying on AB
EG is perpendicular to AB at E
EG is not parallel to DB (proved by contradiction using triangle angle sum)
F is the intersection point of line EG and line BD (or BD produced)
Angles AEF and BEF are both right angles (F on line EG which is perpendicular to AB at E)
F lies on line BD, and since BD is perpendicular to AC at D, angles FDA and FDC are both right angles
F is on line BD (either on same side as B or opposite side of AC)

configuration_map: Configuration: Triangle ABC inscribed in the sought circle, with AC as chord. D is the midpoint of AC on the chord. The perpendicular to AC at D meets the arc at B (making B the midpoint of arc AC). E is the midpoint of AB. F is the intersection of line EG (perpendicular bisector of AB) and line BD (perpendicular bisector of AC). F is the circumcenter of triangle ABC. All right angle claims stem directly from the perpendicularity constructions at D and E. F's position on both perpendicular bisectors simultaneously is established by the non-parallelism proof in Step 4. The proof never uses angle decomposition or inside/outside arguments - it relies solely on SAS congruence from the perpendicular bisector properties.
pass_reason: All spatial claims are mutually consistent. The proof correctly constructs the circumcenter as the intersection of two perpendicular bisectors (of AB and AC), validly proves these lines must intersect via contradiction, and correctly applies SAS twice to establish FA = FB = FC. No angle decomposition issues, no inside/outside contradictions, and no betweenness conflicts arise. The construction is the standard perpendicular bisector method for finding a circumcenter.
